 1            Demetrio Abenoja (“Plaintiff”), individually and on behalf of all others similarly situated,

 2 files this Class Action Complaint against Patelco Credit Union and alleges the following based on

 3 personal knowledge of facts pertaining to him and the investigation of counsel as to all other

 4 matters:

 5                                      NATURE OF THE ACTION

 6            1.     Patelco Credit Union ("Patelco") is one of the largest credit unions in the nation,

 7 servicing communities across Northern California. 1 This class action arises out of a recent

 8 cyberattack and data breach (“Data Breach”) that resulted in the theft and exfiltration by a known

 9 cybercriminal organization who illegally obtained and released the personal data of some Patelco’s
10 retail bank customers on the dark web, including, at a minimum, name, address, contact

11 information, Social Security Number and accounts numbers (“PII”).

12            2.     Patelco's business model involves collecting consumers' PII. This information is
13 retained not only to facilitate the delivery of banking services but also to serve Patelco's business

14 interests and generate profits.

15            3.     Upon information and belief, Patelco made promises and representations to its
16 customers, including Plaintiff and Class Members, that the PII collected from them as a condition

17 of obtaining services at Patelco would be kept safe, confidential, that the privacy of that

18 information would be maintained, and that Patelco would delete any sensitive information after it

19 was no longer required to maintain it.

20            4.     But in June 2024, Patelco failed to protect the information of Patelco customers
21 who entrusted it with their PII. On or about June 29, 2024, Patelco announced, via its website, that

22 Patelco Credit Union experienced a cybersecurity incident that we subsequently confirmed was a

23 ransomware attack. This is a type of cyber-attack where a hacker illegally enters a company’s

24 network, blocks access to some parts, then demands a ransom to resolve the damage they have

25 done. 2

26            5.     By collecting and retaining Plaintiff’s and the Class Members’ PII for its own

27
     1
         https://www.patelco.org/about-patelco/who-we-are
28   2
         https://www.patelco.org/securityupdate
                                                     2

                                       CLASS ACTION COMPLAINT
       Case 4:24-cv-04422-DMR Document 1 Filed 07/22/24 Page 3 of 22




 1 financial benefit, Patelco assumed a duty to Plaintiff and the Class Members to implement and

 2 maintain reasonable and adequate security measures to secure, protect, and safeguard their PII

 3 against unauthorized access and disclosure. Patelco also had a duty to safeguard this PII under

 4 applicable case law, industry standards, and statutory obligations, including Section 5 of the

 5 Federal Trade Commission Act (the “FTC Act”).

 6          6.      But Patelco breached those duties by, among other things, failing to implement and

 7 maintain reasonable security procedures and practices to protect the PII in its possession. The Data

 8 Breach was directly traceable to Patelco’s failure to implement proper security protocols and,

 9 among other things, neglecting to implement adequate and reasonable measures to secure
10 consumers’ data systems against unauthorized intrusions; withholding disclosure regarding

11 insufficiently robust computer systems and security practices to safeguard PII; omitting standard

12 and reasonably available steps to prevent the Data Breach; and inadequately training its staff and

13 employees on proper security measures. Patelco also neglected proper monitoring of its network,

14 which could have detected the intrusion before the thieves exfiltrated the PII or potentially

15 prevented the intrusion altogether.

16          7.      Because of Patelco’s acts and omissions, Plaintiff’s and the Class Members’ PII is
17 now in the hands of Now, Plaintiff and the Class Members must diligently monitor their financial

18 accounts to thwart potential identity theft. They will need to bear out-of-pocket expenses for and

19 spend time on credit monitoring, obtaining identity theft protection, retrieving and reviewing credit

20 reports, and taking other protective measures—both now and in the future. Plaintiff and the Class

21 Members have suffered diminished value to their bargain with Patelco, out-of-pocket expenses

22 associated with protecting their privacy and security, and the value of their time spent addressing

23 or mitigating the effects of the attack.

24          8.      Moreover, Patelco still maintains Plaintiff’s and the Class Members’ PII. Without
25 additional safeguards and independent review, this information remains susceptible to further

26 cyberattacks and theft.

27          9.      Plaintiff and members of the Class have suffered irreparable harm, including the
28 exposure of their PII to nefarious strangers and their significantly increased risk of identity theft.
                                                      3

                                      CLASS ACTION COMPLAINT
        Case 4:24-cv-04422-DMR Document 1 Filed 07/22/24 Page 4 of 22




 1 The information at issue here is the very kind of information that allows identity thieves to

 2 construct false identities and invade all aspects of Plaintiff’s and the Class Members’ lives. In

 3 addition to facing the emotional devastation of having such personal information fall into the

 4 wrong hands, Plaintiff and the Class members must now undertake additional security measures

 5 and precautions to minimize their risk of identity theft. And the ongoing risk to Plaintiff and the

 6 Class Members will persist throughout their lifetimes.

 7                                                PARTIES

 8           10.    Plaintiff Demetrio Abenoja is and at all relevant times has been a citizen of

 9 Discovery Bay, California.
10           11.    Plaintiff has an account with Patelco. Plaintiff provided his PII to Defendant Patelco
11 in connection with his accounts.

12           12.    Plaintiff is deeply concerned about the Data Breach, as his PII is now readily
13 available for cybercriminals to sell, buy, or exchange on the Dark Web.

14           13.    Plaintiff has a continuing interest in ensuring that his PII, which remains in
15 Patelco’s possession, is protected and safeguarded from future breaches.

16           14.    Patelco is a non-profit corporation with its headquarters and principal place of
17 business located at 3 Park Pl., Dublin, California 94568.

18                                    JURISDICTION AND VENUE

19           15.    This Court has original subject matter jurisdiction under the Class Action Fairness

20 Act, 28 U.S.C. § 1332(d)(2), because this is a class action involving more than 100 putative class

21 members and the amount in controversy exceeds $5,000,000, exclusive of interest and costs.

22 Minimal diversity is established because members of the class are citizens of states different than

23 that of Defendant.

24           16.    This Court has personal jurisdiction over Patelco because its principal place of

25 business is located in this District, and it regularly transacts business in this District.

26           17.    Venue is proper in this District under 28 U.S.C. § 1391(a)(1) because Patelco’s

27 principal place of business is located in this District and a substantial part of the events giving rise

28 to this action occurred in this District.
                                                       4

                                       CLASS ACTION COMPLAINT
          Case 4:24-cv-04422-DMR Document 1 Filed 07/22/24 Page 5 of 22




 1                                      FACTUAL ALLEGATIONS

 2           A.     Patelco’s business.

 3           18.     With $9 billion in assets and over 450,000 members nationwide, Patelco is one of

 4 the largest credit unions in the nation. 3

 5           19.    Patelco requires customers to provide their PII to facilitate banking services and for

 6 its own business purposes. In return, Patelco promises to keep consumers' PII secure and not share

 7 it with unauthorized third parties.

 8           20.    Plaintiff and the Class Members entrusted their PII to Patelco with the reasonable

 9 expectation and mutual understanding that Patelco would fulfill its obligations to maintain the
10 confidentiality and security of their information, safeguarding it against unauthorized access. 4

11           B.     Patelco failed to protect Class Members’ private information.

12           21.    Despite Patelco’s assurances that it would employ reasonable measures to

13 safeguard consumers’ PII and only share that information with expressly authorized individuals,

14 Patelco allowed a cybercrime group to infiltrate its systems and steal the PII of its customers.

15           22.    On or about July 1, 2024, Patelco posted a notice to its website concerning the

16 breach (the “Notice”):

17           On June 29, 2024 Patelco Credit Union experienced a ransomware attack.
             Unfortunately, this incident has required us to proactively shut down some of our day-
18           to-day banking systems in order to contain and remediate the issue. Importantly,
             members can still access cash from ATMs. We have engaged a leading third-party
19
             cybersecurity forensic firm to help us to investigate and recover as soon as possible.
20           Please know that our team and third-party partners are working around the clock to
             get back up and running. We are committed to providing transparent and frequent
21           updates to best of our ability as well as the best possible service that we can, given the
             disruption. We sincerely apologize for the inconvenience that this cyber-attack has
22           caused for our members. We anticipate longer than normal wait times and truly
             appreciate your patience and support during this difficult time. 5
23

24           23.    Patelco’s Notice also lacks sufficient details to put consumers on notice of the

25 threats to their privacy. Patelco’s Notice admits that there was “ransomware attack.” Plaintiff and

26

 1 the Class Members remain in the dark about the extent of the data breach; the specific data stolen;

 2 and the measures, if any, being implemented to safeguard their PII moving forward. Indeed,

 3 Patelco’s Notice did not identify the threat actor—or even that the data was stolen. Plaintiff and

 4 the Class Members are left to speculate about the complete ramifications of the Data Breach and

 5 the precise strategies Patelco plans to employ to enhance its information security systems and

 6 monitoring capabilities in order to avert future breaches.

 7           C.     The Data Breach is directly traceable to Patelco’s acts and omissions,

 8                  including its negligence and the breach of its duties to Plaintiff and the Class.

 9           24.    Patelco is responsible for allowing the Data Breach to occur because it failed to
10 implement and maintain reasonable safeguards, failed to comply with industry-standard data

11 security practices, as well as federal and state laws and regulations governing data security, and

12 failed to supervise, monitor, and oversee all third parties it hired who had access to Plaintiff’s and

13 the Class members’ PII.

14           25.    During the Data Breach, Patelco failed to adequately monitor its information
15 technology infrastructure. Had Patelco done so, it would have prevented or mitigated the scope

16 and impact of the Data Breach.

17           26.    By obtaining, collecting, and using Plaintiff’s and the Class Members’ PII, Patelco
18 assumed legal and equitable duties and knew or should have known that it was responsible for

19 protecting Plaintiff’s and the Class Members’ PII from disclosure.

20           27.    Plaintiff’s and the Class Members’ PII was provided to Patelco with the reasonable
21 expectation and understanding that Patelco would comply with its obligations to keep such

22 information confidential and secure from unauthorized access.

23           28.    Cyberattacks have become so prevalent that the FBI and U.S. Secret Service have
24 issued warnings to potential targets, urging them to be aware of and prepared for potential attacks.6

25           29.    Patelco’s data security obligations were particularly important given the substantial

26

27   6
    Ben Kochman, FBI, Secret Service Warn of Targeted Ransomware, Law360 (Nov. 18, 2019),
28 https://www.law360.com/articles/1220974
                                                      6

                                      CLASS ACTION COMPLAINT
          Case 4:24-cv-04422-DMR Document 1 Filed 07/22/24 Page 7 of 22




 1 increase in cyber and ransomware attacks and data breaches in the financial services industries

 2 preceding the date of the Data Breach, as well as given the incredibly sensitive nature of PII that

 3 it retained in its servers.

 4           D.     Patelco failed to comply with FTC guidelines.

 5           30.    The FTC Act, 15 U.S.C. § 45, prohibits Patelco from committing “unfair or

 6 deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.” The Federal Trade Commission (“FTC”)

 7 has determined that a company’s failure to uphold reasonable and appropriate data security for

 8 consumers’ sensitive personal information is an “unfair practice” in violation of the FTC Act.

 9           31.    The FTC has issued guidelines for businesses emphasizing the significance of
10 adopting reasonable data security practices. According to the FTC, integrating data security

11 considerations into all aspects of business decision-making is imperative.

12           32.    In 2016, the FTC issued an updated version of its publication, “Protecting Personal

13 Information: A Guide for Business,” which established cyber-security guidelines for businesses. 7

14 These guidelines underscored the importance for businesses to safeguard personal customer

15 information, securely dispose of unnecessary personal data, encrypt information stored on

16 computer networks, assess network vulnerabilities, and institute policies to address security issues

17 promptly. Additionally, the guidelines recommend using intrusion detection systems to promptly

18 detect breaches, monitoring incoming traffic for signs of hacking attempts, being vigilant about

19 large data transmissions, and having a response plan prepared in the event of a breach. 8

20           33.    The FTC also advises that companies not retain PII longer than necessary for

21 transaction authorization, restrict access to sensitive data, enforce the use of complex passwords

22 on networks, employ industry-tested security methods, monitor the network for suspicious activity,

23 and ensure that third-party service providers have implemented adequate security measures.

24           34.    The FTC has brought enforcement actions against businesses for failing to protect

25

 1 customer data adequately and reasonably, treating the failure to employ reasonable and appropriate

 2 measures to protect against unauthorized access to confidential consumer data as an unfair act or

 3 practice.

 4          35.    Patelco failed to properly implement basic data security practices by failing to

 5 employ reasonable and appropriate measures to protect against unauthorized access to customers’

 6 PII constitutes an unfair act or practice prohibited by Section 5 of the FTC Act, 15 U.S.C. § 45.

 7          36.    Patelco was at all times fully aware of the obligation to protect the PII of customers,

 8 as demonstrated by the existence of its Privacy Policy. Patelco was also aware of the significant

 9 repercussions that would result from their its failure to do so.
10          E.     Patelco failed to comply with industry standards.
11          37.    Companies like Patelco are particularly vulnerable to cyberattacks because of the
12 sensitive nature of the information that they collect and maintain. Because of this vulnerability,

13 and because of the frequency and scale of data breaches in recent years, companies like Patelco

14 that routinely handle and maintain sensitive customer information should, at a minimum,

15 implement industry best practices.

16          38.    These practices include educating and training employees; requiring strong
17 passwords and multi-factor authentication for employees and users; implementing multi-layer

18 security like firewalls, antivirus programs, and anti-malware software; limiting access to sensitive

19 data; backing up and encrypting data; setting up network firewalls; monitoring and limiting

20 network ports; and monitoring and limiting access to physical security systems.

21          39.    Patelco failed to meet the minimum standards of any of the following frameworks
22 laying out industry best practices: the NIST Cybersecurity Framework Version 1.1 (including at a

23 minimum PR.AC-1, PR.AC-3, PR.AC-4, PR.AC-5, PR.AC-6, PR.AC-7, PR.AT-1, PR.DS-1,

24 PR.DS-5, PR.PT-1, PR.PT-3, DE.CM-1, DE.CM-7, DE.CM-8, and RS.CO-2), and the Center for

25 Internet Security’s Critical Security Controls (CIS CSC), which are all established standards in

26 reasonable cybersecurity readiness.

27          40.    These frameworks represent the established industry norms for data security, and
28 Patelco’s failure to adhere to these widely accepted standards caused the Data Breach and has
                                                     8

                                     CLASS ACTION COMPLAINT
       Case 4:24-cv-04422-DMR Document 1 Filed 07/22/24 Page 9 of 22




 1 provided an avenue for criminal exploitation.

 2           F.     Plaintiff and the Class suffered and face substantial risk of future injuries

 3                  because Patelco failed to protect their private information.

 4           41.    As a result of Patelco’s failure to implement and adhere to security measures that

 5 would have protected their PII, Patelco customer PII is now in the hands of criminals, thieves, and

 6 other potentially malicious individuals. Consequently, Plaintiff and the Class Members are at an

 7 elevated risk of identity theft, financial fraud, and other identity-related fraud into the indefinite

 8 future.

 9           42.    Once PII is exposed, it is nearly impossible to ensure the information is fully
10 recovered or protected from future misuse. Thus, Plaintiff and the Class Members must now

11 immediately allocate time, energy, and money to: (1) closely monitor their bills, records, and credit

12 and financial accounts; (2) change login and password information on sensitive accounts more

13 frequently; (3) rigorously screen phone calls, emails, and other communications to avoid social

14 engineering or spear phishing attacks; and (4) search for and subscribe to suitable identity theft

15 protection and credit monitoring services. Plaintiff and the Class Members will need to maintain

16 these heightened protective measures for years, possibly their entire lives, due to Patelco’s actions.

17           43.    Time is a compensable and valuable resource in the United States, and American
18 adults have only 36 to 40 hours of “leisure time” outside of work per week. Usually, this time can

19 be spent at the option of the consumer, but Plaintiff and the Class Members now must spend their

20 leisure time self-monitoring accounts, communicating with financial institutions and credit

21 reporting agencies, contacting government agencies, researching identity protection measures, and

22 implementing self-protection measures that Patelco did not offer.

23           44.    Plaintiff and the Class members have also lost the inherent value of their PII and
24 the value of their bargain with Patelco.

25           45.    PII is a valuable property right. Due to its significant value and the prevalence of
26 large-scale data breaches, identity thieves and cybercriminals have openly posted credit card

27 numbers, Social Security numbers, PII, and other sensitive information on various internet

28 websites, making it publicly accessible. Information from multiple breaches, including the Data
                                                      9

                                      CLASS ACTION COMPLAINT
          Case 4:24-cv-04422-DMR Document 1 Filed 07/22/24 Page 10 of 22




 1 Breach, can be aggregated, increasing its value to thieves and amplifying the potential harm to

 2 victims.

 3           46.    PII can be sold at prices exceeding $1,000. 9 A stolen credit or debit card number

 4 can sell for $15 to $110 on the Dark Web. 10 Criminals can also purchase access to entire company

 5 data breaches for an average cost of between $2,000 to $4,000. 11

 6           47.    Law-abiding consumers place a high value on the privacy of that data. Researchers

 7 shed light on how many consumers value their data privacy—and the amount is considerable.

 8 Indeed, studies confirm that “when privacy information is made more salient and accessible, some

 9 consumers are willing to pay a premium to purchase from privacy protective websites.” 12
10           48.    Accordingly, any company that conducts business with a consumer and
11 subsequently compromises the privacy of their PII effectively deprives that consumer of the full

12 monetary value of their transaction with the company.

13           49.    In sum, due to Patelco’s failures, Plaintiff and the Class Members face a substantial
14 risk of suffering identity theft, fraud, and misuse of their PII, including but not limited to: (a)

15 damage to and diminution in the value of their PII, a form of property that Patelco obtained from

16 Plaintiff and the Class, and loss of their bargain with Patelco; (b) violation of their privacy rights;

17 and (c) ongoing and increased risk of identity theft and fraud, which they must spend time and

18 money mitigating. They have had personal and sensitive PII including, reportedly, credit scores

19 and social security numbers, exposed to the public, resulting in ongoing emotional pain, mental

20 anguish, and embarrassment.

 1                                  CLASS ACTION ALLEGATIONS

 2           50.    Plaintiff repeats and realleges each and every fact, matter, and allegation set forth

 3 above and incorporates them at this point by reference as though set forth in full.

 4           51.    Plaintiff brings this action on behalf of himself and the members of the proposed

 5 Classes, consisting of:

 6           All individuals residing in the United States whose personal identifiable information

 7           was compromised in the Data Breach. (the “Class”).

 8           and,

 9           All individuals residing in California whose personal identifiable information was
10           compromised in the Data Breach (the “California Subclass”).
11 Collectively, (the “Classes”).

12           52.    Excluded from the Class are Patelco, any entity in which Patelco has a controlling
13 interest, and Patelco’s officers, directors, legal representatives, successors, subsidiaries, and

14 assigns. Also excluded from the Class is any judge, justice, or judicial officer presiding over this

15 matter and members of their immediate families and judicial staff.

16           53.    Plaintiff reserves the right to amend the above definition or to propose subclasses
17 before the Court determines whether certification is appropriate.

18           54.    Numerosity: The proposed Class is so numerous that joinder of all members is
19 impracticable. Patelco has acknowledged that the number of class members is at least 751,000.

20           55.    Typicality: Plaintiff’s claims are typical of the claims of the Class. Plaintiff and all
21 members of the Class were injured through Patelco’s uniform misconduct. The same event and

22 conduct that gave rise to Plaintiff’s claims are identical to those that give rise to the claims of every

23 other Class member because Plaintiff and each member of the Class had their sensitive PII

24 compromised in the same way by the same conduct of Patelco.

25           56.    Adequacy: Plaintiff is an adequate representative of the Class because Plaintiff’s
26 interests do not conflict with the interests of the Class; Plaintiff has retained competent counsel

27 who are experienced in prosecuting complex class action and data breach class action litigation;

28 and Plaintiff and Plaintiff’s counsel intend to prosecute this action vigorously. The interests of the
                                                       11

                                       CLASS ACTION COMPLAINT
       Case 4:24-cv-04422-DMR Document 1 Filed 07/22/24 Page 12 of 22




 1 Class will be fairly and adequately protected by Plaintiff and Plaintiff’s counsel.

 2          57.    Superiority: A class action is superior to all other available methods for the fair

 3 and efficient adjudication of this lawsuit because individual litigation of the claims of all members

 4 of the Class is economically unfeasible and procedurally impracticable. The injury suffered by

 5 each individual member of the Class is relatively small in comparison to the burden and expense

 6 of individual prosecution of litigation. It would be very difficult for members of the Class to

 7 effectively redress Patelco’s wrongdoing. Further, individualized litigation presents a potential for

 8 inconsistent or contradictory judgments.

 9          58.    Commonality and Predominance: There are numerous questions of law and fact
10 common to the Class which predominate over any questions affecting only individual members of

11 the Class.

12          59.    Among the questions of law and fact common to the Class are:
13          •      Whether Patelco engaged in the wrongful conduct alleged herein;
14          •      Whether Patelco failed to adequately safeguard Plaintiff’s and the Class’s PII;
15          •      Whether Patelco owed a duty to Plaintiff and the Class to adequately protect their
